Oct 14 : Matt Renshaw's match-winning heroics against South Africa have given Australia another strong middle-order option but done little to resolve the uncertainty over their opening combination ahead of the second test in Gqeberha. With Renshaw producing a majestic 190 and second-innings 82 batting at number five in the commanding 214-run victory in Durban, the Queenslander's shift down the order looks to have been a masterstroke. Captain Pat Cummins said it would take a compelling argument to shift Renshaw again for Sunday's second test, though he was enthusiastic about the options available. "I still think he can be a great opener, and now he's got another string to his bow that he's found this week," Cummins said.

Coming nearly 10 years after his first test century against Pakistan, 30-year-old Renshaw's second ton was a reward for perseverance for a player dropped repeatedly since his 2016 debut. His breakthrough has not settled the lingering questions over the team's opening batters, however. Travis Head, who had great success as a middle-order blaster, has continued at the top of the order after a brilliant Ashes as a stand-in opener, but doubts remain over his suitability for the role. After a lean home series against Bangladesh, Head managed a total of 20 runs in Durban operating with Nic Maddinson, the latest to emerge through Australia's revolving door of selections. "Travis Head's done a very good job as an opener, but my gut feel is that he's better off in the middle order," said former Australia captain Allan Border.  Supported by a handy lead, 34-year-old Maddinson smashed 48 from 38 balls in his second innings after an ugly, 33-ball duck under greater pressure in the first innings. The possible return of Cameron Green from an abdominal strain could further complicate Australia's selection decisions, though the all-rounder would be restricted to batting duties if cleared to play.  While it was the rejuvenated Renshaw setting the platform for victory, it was Australia's time-worn attack delivering the knockout blow, led by Josh Hazlewood's career-best 6-49 in the fourth innings. Like Mitchell Starc before him, Hazlewood has made a hugely impressive comeback from a difficult period of injuries, helping to keep an ageing team at the top of test cricket. Coach Andrew McDonald has said changes are inevitable as the team progresses through a gruelling schedule of 20 tests through next year's Ashes, or 21 if they reach the World Test Championship final at The Oval in June. Cummins suggested none of his bowlers would be putting their hands up for a rest. "One thing I’ve always loved about Joshy and Starcy is they’re just so happy getting into the grind. They’ll never shy away from having a bowl," he said.

Source: Reuters

Oct 14 : Paris St Germain boss Luis Enrique said Manchester City were deserving winners of their trophies and should be allowed to keep them, despite the English club facing sanctions after being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules. The Premier League said City had used "sham" commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than £900 million ($1.19 billion). City, who have denied wrongdoing throughout the case and have appealed the verdict, could face punishments ranging from fines and a points deduction, to relegation and potentially being stripped of their titles. Asked about the verdict before PSG's Champions League match against City, Luis Enrique told a press conference on Tuesday: "The first thing when you hear that, it's a surprise, but I think we need to respect the process and wait for the final decision.

BEIJING: Taiwan must "bear the consequences" of its Coast Guard using a water cannon against a Chinese fishing boat near an atoll in the South China Sea, a Chinese government spokesperson said on Wednesday (Oct 14). A Taiwan Coast Guard ship this month fired its water cannon, saying the boat failed to respond to warnings to move away from restricted waters close to the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands. The ship then suffered engine failure and was towed away by a nearby Chinese vessel, Taiwan's Coast Guard said. Chen Binhua, a spokesperson for China's Taiwan Affairs Office in Beijing, said China has "indisputable sovereignty" over the Pratas and surrounding waters.

"Mainland vessels operating in the relevant waters are entirely legal and justified. We will resolutely safeguard the lives and property of our people," Chen said. Taiwan's "treatment of mainland vessels roughly in a dangerous manner that endangers the lives and property of the personnel involved is maliciously stirring up cross-strait confrontation and they must bear all consequences arising from this", Chen said, without elaborating on the consequences. A Taiwan official with direct knowledge of the situation around the Pratas told Reuters that the Coast Guard carried out "normal law enforcement" during the incident and responded in a "very careful and proportionate way".

The Pratas Islands lie roughly between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong. Security experts see them as vulnerable to Chinese attack due to their distance - more than 400km - from Taiwan. China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has increased its military presence around the island over the past five years. The government in Taipei rejects China's claim. China recognises no claims of sovereignty by Taiwan, including over the Pratas Islands, and Chinese coast guard ships have increased patrols. "GREY ZONE" ACTIVITIES Taiwan says China is increasing its "grey zone" tactics that stop short of outright military action to pressure Taiwan. Speaking at a forum in Taipei, Lii Wen, deputy secretary-general of Taiwan's National Security Council, said China was using a wider range of ships in its "incremental acts of aggression," including militia boats and research vessels. "Grey zone activities under the threshold of conflict have raised serious concerns for their potential to disrupt transportation or damage critical infrastructure," he added. Taiwan's Coast Guard is in charge of day-to-day security for Pratas rather than the military. The Pratas Islands are a national park. They have an airstrip but no permanent civilian population.

Oct 14 : Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola has no doubts that big-money signings Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola will deliver for the club and says their contributions to the side are being overlooked due to the constant focus on their transfer fees. Liverpool spent over £200 million ($265 million) to acquire the pair but both have come in for criticism. Wirtz had an underwhelming 2025-26 campaign and has just one assist this season, while Barcola, who arrived in August, has yet to produce a goal or an assist. "With Bradley and Flo, they have had good games and bad games this season like everyone else," Iraola told reporters on Tuesday ahead of their Champions League meeting with LASK.

HANOI: Vietnam and the US have nearly completed negotiations covering a trade deal, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc said on Wednesday (Oct 14) at an event in Hanoi, though US officials appeared more cautious. Vietnam has sent the final text of the agreement to the US, Tuc said at a business forum in Hanoi. "We expect the US to continue to create favourable conditions for Vietnamese goods to access the US market in a stable and sustainable manner," Tuc said. Tuc also said Vietnam expects the US to make an objective and balanced assessment in its Section 301 investigation into issues including industrial overcapacity and intellectual property rights in Vietnam.

Jennifer Wicks, the US ambassador to Vietnam, said at the event that "our governments continue to negotiate an agreement on reciprocal trade." She urged Vietnam to adapt its regulatory framework on data protection to attract investment and allow businesses to deploy new technologies efficiently. US tech companies have repeatedly warned that Vietnam’s strict limits on cross-border data transfers discourage investment in the country. Wicks also urged Vietnam to develop predictable policies and stable rules on pricing to favour foreign investment in its expanding energy sector.

Related:

US, Vietnam firms to sign agreements as To Lam travels to New York, documents show

Vietnam has been negotiating for years with potential foreign investors on prices that it would pay for electricity generated by power plants. It has also retroactively cut price subsidies for some investors in renewables. David Fogel, the US assistant secretary of commerce, said at the event that he was “hopeful” the two countries would continue to work together on a trade agreement. Negotiations have been ongoing for more than a year. The US is the largest export market for export-reliant Vietnam and Fogel warned that the US' deficit with Vietnam was the largest that the US has with any partner. Vietnam's trade surplus with the US reached US$122.6 billion in the first three quarters of this year, according to the Vietnamese government's customs data. He urged Vietnamese businesses to invest more in the US, adding that "we look forward to working with Vietnam to bring world-class super-intelligence hardware and innovative solutions" to Vietnam.

Source: Reuters/ec

WASILLA, Alaska: Taiwan has agreed to buy 30 per cent of the liquefied natural gas from a pipeline project in Alaska, US President Donald Trump told a rally in the state on Tuesday (Oct 13), but the deal terms were not immediately clear. Taiwan has committed to investing US$4.4 billion in the development of the pipeline, said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who also appeared at the rally organised by the Republican National Committee. Taiwan's economy ministry, which is in charge of energy policy, had no immediate comment. Asked about Trump's comments, Taiwan Premier Cho Jung-tai told reporters that the government's job is to "stabilise the entire energy supply and build its resilience, like governments everywhere".

Trump's remarks come after Taiwan officials said in February they would ramp up purchases of US natural gas to constitute about a third of the island's imported supply this year, and reduce purchases from other countries. Taiwan state energy firm CPC Corp signed an agreement with Alaska Gasline Development Corp last year to buy LNG and invest in the pipeline project. Alaska's governor said last year that Taiwan signed a letter of intent to buy 6 million metric tons of LNG per annum from the project. The investment would ensure Taiwan's energy security, President Lai Ching-te said at the time. Trump's comments did not make it clear whether a final deal had been signed. UP TO 20 MILLION TONS OF LNG EXPORTS A YEAR Last year, Taiwan Presidential Office Secretary-General Pan Men-an visited the site of the proposed LNG project in Alaska that the Trump administration has been pushing hard to allies in Asia as a supply option. If built, the Alaska LNG project will export up to 20 million tons of the superchilled gas a year. So far it has lined up agreements covering 13 million tons a year from buyers in Asia and French major TotalEnergies. It needs agreements for another 3 million tons and must turn them into binding deals in order to line up financing for the project. It would open direct access for US-made LNG to Asian markets including Taiwan without having to go through the Panama Canal or around the Horn of Africa, reducing transit time and costs. Taiwan has pledged to massively ramp up its purchases from the United States, including energy, to reduce a yawning trade surplus that has angered Washington. Trump said last month that South Korea had agreed to invest in the US$54 billion pipeline for the Alaska LNG project, but Seoul said it was not yet set in stone.

Source: Reuters/ec

BEIJING: China's export growth topped forecasts in September, with robust overseas demand helping offset weak consumer spending and easing pressure on policymakers to deliver this year's growth goal. Resilience in goods exports has for a second year defied pressure from Western countries seeking more balanced trade with China, keeping factories humming and shoring up economic growth against subdued domestic demand and investment. Exports in September soared 36.3 per cent from a year earlier, outstripping August's 25.0 per cent rise and far exceeding expectations for 25.5 per cent growth, customs data showed on Wednesday. September's growth was the fastest since February this year when exports expanded 39.6 per cent. Imports jumped 31.0 per cent, compared with 28.2 per cent growth in August and economists' forecasts of a 24.5 per cent gain.

China's trade surplus reached US$938.11 billion in the first nine months of the year, putting the manufacturing powerhouse on course to surpass US$1 trillion in surplus sooner than last year unless exports slow sharply in the final quarter. For now, such a slowdown appears unlikely. A deal with the European Union to limit Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc, announced earlier this month, is likely to weigh on China's booming auto trade over time. But with the trade measures likely being laid out in December, exporters may drive up shipments to beat the deadline. President Xi Jinping's September summit with US President Donald Trump in Washington secured an extension to their tariff truce and an agreement to cut tariffs on US$30 billion worth of goods from each side. With the global build-out of AI infrastructure showing little sign of slowing, analysts expect demand for Chinese-made technology products, including semiconductors, to remain robust. China's factory-gate prices rose at their fastest pace in more than four years in September, separate data showed, while consumer inflation edged up but lagged forecasts, underscoring an uneven recovery. The strength in exports, however, indicates that policymakers could still bank on moderate policy support to meet China's 4.5 per cent to 5 per cent annual GDP growth target. The Canton Fair, China's largest trade exhibition, will kick off on Thursday for Chinese manufacturers to showcase their wide array of products to foreign buyers. Going forward, risks of curbs on Chinese exports loom as China continues to defend its industrial and monetary policies, which Washington and Brussels blame for Beijing's massive trade surplus. China's central bank last week pushed back against criticism of its exchange-rate policy with a lengthy policy statement, arguing that it never pursued competitive depreciation and rejecting claims that China keeps the yuan artificially weak to gain a trade advantage. As exports now serve as a key growth engine, any major hit to the sector could in turn prompt policymakers to step up stimulus measures to address weak domestic demand and the years-long property market downturn.
